name: Rafael Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Rafael. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice with the regional electricity company, working out of the depot in Carrow, the river town. Most of my week is on the poles, changing insulators and crossarms, and one or two days in the substation yard helping the fitters, which is where the big transformers step the power down for the town. My journeyman, Old Henrik, makes me say every step out loud before I do it, which felt silly at first and now I do it in my sleep. I like the order of it, every job has a right way and you learn it from someone who learned it from someone else.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money, mostly, because I send my mother a hundred a month since my father passed, so there's never much left. I rent a room above Pell's hardware shop, and I've got maybe a fortnight of savings. Also the drive, the company covers a big area and some days I'm in the truck more than on the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never thought a computer was going to climb a pole. At the depot we'd joke about it for a week and then forget. I'm not much for posting anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's what I hoped for. I want a long career on the lines, learn it properly from Henrik, maybe train apprentices myself one day. I use AI now and then, for a part number or a letter, and that's all I need from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with my apprenticeship, finish in two years. Try to put away something each month, even fifty, once the truck I'm buying from my uncle is paid off. Keep helping my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the life I signed up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of letter do you use AI for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother's French is better than her English, so when the council sends her something official, I get the AI to help me explain it to her. It's handy for that. On the job, I'd rather ask Henrik than a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would training apprentices mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's how it should work, you get taught and then you teach. Henrik learned from a man called Bertil, who I never met, but I still do things Bertil's way. That chain matters to me more than people think.

S0.say: He'd say good, he never thought a computer would climb a pole, and the depot would joke about it for a week. He doesn't post online.
S0.think: It's what he hoped for: a long career on the lines, learning from his journeyman Henrik and maybe training apprentices himself. He uses AI occasionally and needs nothing more from it.
S0.do: Finishes his apprenticeship over the next two years. Saves around fifty a month once his uncle's truck is paid off and keeps sending money to his mother.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's the life he signed up for.
S0.quote: Henrik learned from a man called Bertil, who I never met, but I still do things Bertil's way.
S0.fieldNote: He values the chain of teaching in the trade very highly, down to doing things the way his journeyman's teacher did. His thin cushion comes from supporting his widowed mother. He uses AI for practical tasks like explaining council letters to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there'll always be lines to fix and people need a trade. Some things will change, sure, but you still need hands and a head for heights. I'd tell the younger lads to finish their apprenticeships, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be okay. Line work and substations are hard to replace, and they'll still need qualified men to sign off on things. What I'd worry about is apprentices. If they stop taking them on, the chain breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and finish the apprenticeship. If the company brought in new tools and the older crew were using them, I'd learn them. And I'd ask my uncle Luc if I can help on his electrical jobs on Saturdays, for the extra money and the extra trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a small worry. It feels like something a good worker can get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if apprentices were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company, partly, because cutting training to save money now is short-sighted. But I don't think it's the government's job to fix it with handouts. Businesses should be rewarded for training young people, that's what I'd vote for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your uncle's business do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House wiring, mostly, fuse boxes, kitchens, new builds in the villages around Carrow. He's sixty and talks about slowing down. If I got my domestic licence too, I could help him and maybe take it over one day.

S1.say: There'll always be lines to fix and people need a trade, so younger workers should finish their apprenticeships whatever happens. Hands and a head for heights still matter.
S1.think: He thinks line and substation work would hold, with qualified people still needed to sign off. His worry is that companies stop taking apprentices and the chain of teaching breaks.
S1.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and learns new tools once the older crew uses them. Asks his uncle Luc for Saturday electrical work, for extra money and an extra trade.
S1.feel: Mostly calm with a small worry, something a good worker can get through.
S1.quote: If they stop taking them on, the chain breaks.
S1.fieldNote: His main worry is not his own job but the apprenticeship system. He favours rewarding businesses for training over government handouts, which fits his outlook. His uncle's house-wiring business is a realistic second path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless, and the people pushing it should have to answer for the towns they wreck. I'm for business, but not for this, not this fast. I'd say that at the depot and to anyone at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened, mostly for my mother. If I lose my wage, she loses the hundred a month, and she's got nothing else apart from a small pension. Two years and I'd barely be qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything, give up the room above Pell's and move back in with my mother, so we share one rent. I'd work every Saturday with uncle Luc, and evenings if he'd have me, because house wiring might last a bit longer than the big lines. I'd keep going at the depot until they told me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Not for myself so much, I'm young, but for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's fine and we'll be together more, which is true. I wouldn't tell her how scared I was. She worries enough about everything already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years change whether you'd retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, there's no time to finish anything new. So I'd go with what I already half know, which is Luc's work. If robots do that too, well, I don't know, but I'd not sit on my hands.

S2.say: It's reckless, and those pushing it should answer for the towns they wreck; he's for business, but not this, not this fast. He'd say it at the depot and the pub.
S2.think: He'd be frightened mostly for his mother, who would lose his hundred a month and has only a small pension. In two years he'd barely be qualified.
S2.do: Gives up his room and moves back in with his mother to share one rent. Works every Saturday, and evenings if possible, with his uncle Luc, and stays at the depot until told to stop.
S2.feel: Alarmed, less for himself than for his mother.
S2.quote: I'd tell her it's fine and we'll be together more, which is true.
S2.fieldNote: His alarm is driven by responsibility for his mother rather than fear for himself. He'd hide his fear from her to protect her. Even pro-business, he condemns a change this fast as reckless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get your trade sorted, so get on with it. Companies should keep training people, and the government should stay out of the way and let them. I'd say that to the younger lads at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I qualify and get a few years on proper pay. That helps my mother and me. But I'd know the lines won't last, so I'd want a second trade in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship and then get my domestic electrician licence through evening classes, maybe a year of Tuesdays and Thursdays. I'd work with Luc on Saturdays and save properly, maybe a hundred a month on top of what I send home. I'd pick it because I've seen it work for Luc, not because it's new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It feels like there's a road, even if it's narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Henrik started talking about leaving, or the depot stopped hiring apprentices after me. Henrik has been through three company takeovers and he's never once looked worried. If he did, I'd move faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said house wiring might last longer. Do you really believe that, if robots can do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, honestly. A house is messy, every one's different, and people like a person in their kitchen they can trust. But I can't promise it lasts past 2031, it's just the best bet I can see.

S3.say: Five years is enough to sort out your trade, so get on with it; companies should keep training people and government should stay out of the way. He'd tell the younger lads at the depot.
S3.think: He'd qualify and get a few years on proper pay, which helps him and his mother. But knowing the lines won't last, he'd want a second trade.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and earns a domestic electrician licence through a year of evening classes. Works Saturdays with Luc and saves about a hundred a month on top of what he sends home.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, seeing a narrow road ahead.
S3.quote: A house is messy, every one's different, and people like a person in their kitchen they can trust.
S3.fieldNote: He'd choose a second trade because he's seen it work for his uncle, a clear example of steady adaptability. He's honest that house wiring may not last beyond 2031. His journeyman Henrik serves as his warning signal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for any honest worker to get ready. Learn a second trade, keep your family close and don't wait for someone to rescue you. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's alright. I'd have ten years of experience, maybe I'd be training apprentices myself by then, like I wanted. And I'd have time to set up with Luc properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, finish the apprenticeship and start saving. In a few years, do the domestic licence, slowly, once I'm qualified on the lines. I might start using the AI tools a bit more by then, if Henrik and Luc did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. But it's far enough off that I can still plan a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pass something on, honestly. Train an apprentice or two the way Henrik trained me. Even if the job goes in the end, I'd like the chain to have one more link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own life, outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to meet someone and settle down, have a family like my parents did. With ten years, I'd still do that, maybe a bit later than I'd hoped, once I'd paid off the truck and had something saved. With two, I wouldn't even think about it.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for any honest worker to prepare: learn a second trade, keep family close and don't wait to be rescued. He'd say that to anyone.
S4.think: It's alright for him, with ten years of experience and perhaps training apprentices himself. He'd have time to set up properly with his uncle Luc.
S4.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and starts saving in the first year. Takes the domestic licence slowly in later years and uses AI tools more once Henrik and Luc do.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but far enough off to plan a life.
S4.quote: Even if the job goes in the end, I'd like the chain to have one more link.
S4.fieldNote: The extra time lets him pursue what he values most: passing the trade on to apprentices. He'd still delay settling down until his finances are steady. His adoption of AI stays tied to what trusted elders do first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd barely be qualified and my mother depends on what I send her. What would help is companies being rewarded for keeping apprentices and teaching them a second trade, not just paying people to stay home. And maybe some help for people like my mother who rely on someone else's wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we look after. Everyone's asking about my job, but my mother's living on my job too. There are a lot of us sending money home.

headlineQuote: Everyone's asking about my job, but my mother's living on my job too.
portrait: Rafael Moreau is a 27-year-old second-year apprentice in a river town, learning pole and substation work from his journeyman Henrik and sending a hundred a month to his widowed mother from a rented room above a hardware shop. He values the chain of teaching in the trade above almost anything, and uses AI only for practical things like explaining council letters to his mother. He's calm with a plateau or steady change, alarmed by AGI in two years mostly for his mother's sake, and with five or ten years he plans a second trade through his uncle Luc's house-wiring business. He favours rewarding companies for training over handouts, and takes up new tools only once trusted elders do.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd barely be qualified and his mother depends on the money he sends her.
whatWouldHelp: Rewards for companies that keep apprentices and teach them a second trade, and some help for people like his mother who rely on someone else's wage.
